en: The Mahābherī-haraka Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of hundreds of thousands of great bodhisattvas; furthermore, there were numerous assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas; additionally, there were hundreds of thousands of assemblies of upāsakas and upāsikās; and further, there were the Brahmā kings, Śakra the lord of devas, and the hosts of the four heavenly kings who rule over the Sahā world, as well as immeasurable numbers of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached this Dharma to those four assemblies:

"Where there is existence, there is suffering and pleasure; where there is no existence, there is neither suffering nor pleasure. Therefore, to be free from suffering and pleasure is the supreme bliss of Nirvāṇa."
Those five hundred śrāvaka bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions;
whose minds had attained mastery like great dragons, having attained excellent liberation of mind and excellent liberation through wisdom;
who had accomplished what was to be done and laid down the heavy burden—
Having attained their own benefit and exhausted all fetters of existence, they were liberated in mind through right knowledge—attaining the foremost *pāramitā* of sovereign mastery over all minds.
There were immeasurable students who all attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, and *anāgāmin*.

There was an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus who had accomplished the outflow-tainted dharmas, and a host of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had accomplished immeasurable asaṃkhyeya merits, arriving from the ten directions in numbers beyond the reach of calculation or analogy, and which could not be known even by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

With the exception of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva—such leading Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas and an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya multitude—as the grasses and trees produced by the great earth, so too were the multitudes of Bodhisattvas who had come from all directions, beyond all calculation.
Furthermore, there was the bhikṣuṇī Kṣema together with the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs; Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ and Queen Mallikā, each accompanied by immeasurable great retinues;
and the elder Sudatta together with various upāsakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma-gate of existence and non-existence amidst the great assembly.
Then, King Prasenajit rose from his reclining position and thought to himself:
"I should now go to where the World-Honored One is."
Having thought this, he immediately set out, beat the drums and blew the conch shells, and went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason], asked intentionally: "Ānanda!"
"For what reason are there the sounds of drums and conchs?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "King Prasenajit has come to the place where the Buddha is; these are the sounds of his beating drums and blowing conchs."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You, too, should now beat the great Dharma drum; I shall now preach the Mahādharmabherī Sūtra.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have never heard the name of this *Mahābherīhāraka-sūtra*.
For what reason is it called the *Mahābherīhāraka-sūtra*?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"By what means do you know this?
Even these great bodhisattvas who have gathered here cannot know the six-syllable name of this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra; how much less could you possibly hear or know it?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented.”
"The name of this Dharma is truly difficult to know.
"It is so, Ānanda; it is indeed thus and not otherwise."
“Ānanda! This Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra is rare in the world, like the udumbara flower.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Do not all Buddhas possess this Dharma?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
“All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess this Dharma.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that is so, for what reason have all those bodhisattvas, the heroes among men, come together here in such great assembly?”
"For what reason do those Tathāgatas not themselves preach [this] in their own lands?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is like a certain aranyaka bhikṣu who dwells in seclusion within a mountain cave."
When the time came, he entered the village intending to beg for food; however, along the way he saw various corpses of humans and animals.
Having seen them, he conceived a sense of revulsion and returned without eating, saying:
"Alas, what suffering! What misery!"
"That is indeed as it should be.
At another time, his mind attaining joy, he thought to himself:
"I shall go once more to observe a corpse, so as to increase my sense of revulsion and detachment."
"Furthermore, he went toward a village to seek out a corpse and cultivate the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
Having seen it, he investigated it and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Thus, the Buddhas of other directions do not preach impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or impurity."
Why is this? Such is the natural law of all Buddha-fields.
Those Tathāgatas speak thus to the bodhisattvas:
"How marvelous is this difficult feat!

The World-Honored One Śākyamuni has appeared in this world of the five turbidities and, for the sake of sentient beings afflicted by suffering, has preached the Mahābherī-haraka Sūtra through various skillful means."
"Therefore, sons of good family, you should train yourselves in this way.
Those bodhisattvas have all come to this assembly because they desire to see me, pay their respects, and prostrate before me.
Having already come to this assembly, some have attained the first stage, up to the tenth stage.
For this reason, the Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra is extremely difficult to encounter;
for this reason, the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions have all gathered here to hear the Dharma.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Welcome to all;
they have all attained this rare Dharma of the sutra.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"A profound sūtra such as this is not for everyone.
Therefore, one should not say: [that it is common to all]."
"Welcome to all. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is it that they are not 'welcome to all'?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is the secret Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas; it is profoundly deep and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to believe."
Therefore, Ānanda, you should not say: "Welcome to all."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Is it not like when King Prasenajit strikes a great war drum while on the battlefield; does the sound cause all arrows to fall away from those who hear it?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When King Prasenajit beats the drum for battle, it is not the case that all who hear the sound of the drum rejoice.
There are those who are timid and weak; upon hearing it, they are terrified, as if facing death or its proximity."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
This Dharma-door called the *Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra* is one that those of the two vehicles do not believe in.
For this reason, Ānanda!
Just as that king strikes the great royal drum when it is time for battle,
so too this Great Dharma Drum— the secret of all Buddhas— is proclaimed only when a Buddha appears in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Are these bhikṣus pure and uniform, truly powerful, free from all dregs and chaff, and capable of hearing this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra?"
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu who violates the precepts and transgresses the Vinaya, he is one whom Mahāmaudgalyāyana would rebuke.
If such a person exists, I would not associate with him, much less would the World-Honored One."
"The assembly gathered here now is like a grove of sandalwood—pure and uniform.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Although this assembly is entirely pure and uniform, they do not yet understand well the teachings given in concealment."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by ‘hidden and concealed teaching’?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Speaking with concealment means saying that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate nirvāṇa, whereas in reality the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and does not perish; parinirvāṇa is not a phenomenon of destruction."
This sūtra is free from obscuration and pure; it clarifies its voice through hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions, analyzing and revealing its meaning. Therefore, Kāśyapa!
"You should further observe this great assembly.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again observed those who had come, considering how they had arrived.

In an instant, sentient beings of inferior faith, as well as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice, reflected upon their own inadequacy and gave rise to thoughts of retreat and abandonment.
For example, among a multitude of royal wrestlers, there was one known as "The Thousand-Wrestler" who rose from his seat, struck a drum, and proclaimed:
"Who is able to withstand me in a contest of strength?"
Those who were unable [to do so] remained silent, thinking to themselves:
"I am not capable of contending with him in strength; he might injure me or even cause my death."
Within that assembly, there was no one who dared to oppose him; thus he was named the Valiant and Invincible Malla, who raised the great banner of victory.
In this way, inferior beings, as well as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas at the beginning of their practice, thought to themselves:
"I am not capable of receiving [this teaching]; the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, yet he further speaks of his eternal abiding and non-extinction."
"In this great assembly, I have heard what I have never heard before.
Having said this, he rose from his seat and departed. Why was this?
Those individuals have long cultivated the view of emptiness regarding parinirvāṇa; having heard this sūtra on purity that is free from concealment, they rise from their seats and depart.

Of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of initial practice who had come from the ten directions—numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas—only one part remains. These are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who resolve upon the eternal and unchanging nature of the dharmakāya; they alone dwell securely in the upholding of all Tathāgatagarbha sūtras, and are able to explain, console, and provide understanding for the world regarding all teachings on concealed truths.

They skillfully contemplate all sūtras of definitive and provisional meaning, being able to subdue those who violate the precepts; they revere and follow those who are pure and virtuous, attaining great pure faith in the Mahāyāna, and never conceiving thoughts of superiority toward the two vehicles.

Setting aside such Mahāyāna sūtras as these, no other sūtras are spoken; it is taught only that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and that there is the tathāgatagarbha. Yet, this does not abandon emptiness, nor is it the emptiness of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi); rather, it is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all those conditioned phenomena.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Ask the great assembly once more:
'Do you all wish to hear this Great Dharma Drum Vaipulya One Vehicle, namely, the Mahāyāna Sūtra that is difficult to believe?'"
Thus he spoke up to three times.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having circumambulated him three times to the right, he addressed the great assembly:
"Do you all wish to hear this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra?"
"The Tathāgata shall now universally expound for you all the One Vehicle—namely, the Mahāyāna, which transcends the realms of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Thus he spoke three times, and they all replied:
"We wish and desire to hear it."
"O Mahākāśyapa! We have all come for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
How excellent! Out of compassion, please preach the Mahābherī-haraka Sūtra for us."
Kāśyapa spoke again: “How do you believe?
They replied immediately:
“It is as if there were a man, barely twenty years of age, who had a son one hundred years old.
If the Buddha speaks thus, we too shall follow and believe accordingly.”
How much more so, then, would one fail to believe and accept the True Dharma when it is preached? Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata acts in accordance with what he teaches.
“The Tathāgata’s pure eye illuminates all without obstruction; with his Buddha-eye, he perceives and knows our minds.
Kāśyapa exclaimed, “Excellent, excellent!”
"Virtuous ones! You are capable of listening to the Mahābherī-hāraka Sūtra, whether to uphold it or to expound it.
Thus the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Just as there might be a man twenty years of age who has a son one hundred years old, so too is it with the Mahābherī-hāraka-parivarta Sūtra.
Why is this? Because although the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, he is also eternally abiding; and although all things are without self, he speaks of a self."
He then replied: "Only the Buddha can know this.
We shall receive and uphold it exactly as the World-Honored One has spoken."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Great Dharma Drum Sūtra, beat the Great Dharma Drum, and blow the Great Dharma Conch.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
Listen now as I expound the Mahābherī-hāraka Sūtra.”
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
For what reason?”
Because this is my domain,
the Tathāgata regards me with great respect.
What constitutes this respect?
He once said to me,
"Come and sit with me.
For this reason, I ought to recognize his kindness.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Kāśyapa! For this reason, I treat you with respect."
Kāśyapa! It is like King Prasenajit, who skillfully maintains the fourfold army; when engaged in battle, he beats the great war drum and blows the great war conch, standing firm against the enemy.
"Out of gratitude for this nurturing care, he will exert his full strength in battle, enabling him to defeat his enemies and bring peace to the borders of the kingdom.
In this same way, monks!
After my parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa shall protect and uphold this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra."
For this reason, I share half of my seat with him.
Therefore, he shall practice what I have practiced, and after my parinirvāṇa, he will be capable of widely proclaiming the Mahādharmabherī-sūtra.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I am the eldest son born from the mouth of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Just as King Prasenajit instructs his princes in the various fields of knowledge so that they may be capable of succeeding to the royal lineage in future generations, even so, bhikṣus!"
After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa will protect and uphold this sutra in just the same way. Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
it is like King Prasenajit, who frequently enters into enmity with many other kings and repeatedly attacks and wages war against them.

At various times, those warriors—the fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—upon hearing the sound of the great drum, felt no fear in their hearts and firmly grasped their armor and weapons.
At that time, the king showed him great favor and bestowed many gifts upon him.
When the time for battle arrived, he further granted him precious treasures and cities.
If he were able to defeat the enemy, the king would crown him with white silk and enfeoff him as a king.
In this way, Kāśyapa, when my disciples—

monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— train in accordance with the precepts, achieve perfection in the Prātimokṣa, and dwell well within the discipline, the Tathāgata bestows peace and happiness upon gods and humans.
Those who have performed great merit and subdued the four māras shall have their heads crowned with the white silk of liberation through the Four Noble Truths.

If there are those with superior faith and understanding who seek the Great Self and the eternally abiding Dharmakāya of the Buddha-treasury, the Tathāgata at that time shall pour the water of sarvajñā (omniscience) upon their crowns and crown their heads with the white silk of the Mahāyāna.
Mahākāśyapa! I now do likewise;
with a silken scarf of the Mahāyāna, I crown your head, so that you shall protect and uphold this sutra in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the future.
“Kāśyapa, you should know that after my parinirvāṇa, you are capable of protecting and upholding such sūtras as these.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I shall do as the World-Honored One instructs.”
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forth, and even after my parinirvāṇa, I shall constantly protect, uphold, and extensively expound this sutra.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!
I shall now expound for you the Mahābherī-hāraka Sūtra.
At that time, the hosts of devas and nāgas in the void raised their voices in unison and exclaimed:
“Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!

Today the devas have rained down celestial flowers, and the hosts of nāga kings have rained down ambrosial water and fine powdered incense, bringing comfort and joy to all sentient beings. You should be established by the World-Honored One as his eldest son of the Dharma.”
Then the assembly of devas and nāgas spoke in unison with these verses:
“In the city of Śrāvastī, the king beats the drum and blows the war-shell;
In the Jeta Grove, the Dharma King strikes the great Dharma drum.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should now strike the great Dharma drum with the mallet of inquiry; the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, shall speak for you, and the God among Gods shall resolve your doubts."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"There is a bhikṣu named Great Vaipulya Faith; if any of the fourfold assembly hears his name, the arrows of greed, anger, and delusion will all be extracted."
Why is this so? Kāśyapa!
It is, for example, like King Prasenajit, who had a son of Jīvaka named Uttara-bhaiṣajya.
When King Prasenajit was at war with a hostile kingdom, he addressed his chief physician, saying:
"Bring me quickly the medicine that can extract arrows from sentient beings."
At that time, the Senior Physician took an anti-poison medicine and the King smeared it upon his battle drum;

whether by smearing, fumigating, or beating it, if any sentient beings were struck by poisoned arrows, upon hearing the sound of that drum—whether from a distance of one yojana or two—the arrows would all be extracted.
In this way, Kāśyapa!
If there are those who hear and believe the name of a bhikṣu of the Vaipulya [sūtras], the arrows of greed, anger, and ignorance will all be extracted. Why is this?
By means of this sutra, he expands and propagates the True Dharma; because he has achieved perfection in this present life, he attains this great fruit. Mahākāśyapa!

You should observe that even an ordinary drum, though devoid of consciousness, possesses such power to benefit sentient beings when treated with unconscious medicinal substances—whether by being smeared, fumigated, or struck.
"How much more so, then, when one hears the name of that bhikṣu who has faith in the Vaipulya sūtras—could he not eliminate the three poisons of sentient beings?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If merely hearing the name of a bodhisattva can eliminate the three kinds of poisonous arrows for sentient beings, how much more so when one invokes the name and merit of the World-Honored One, saying 'Namo Śākyamuni'?"

If merely praising the merit of Śākyamuni’s name can extract the three kinds of poisonous arrows from sentient beings, how much more so for hearing this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra and being comforted by its exposition, whether in verses or in prose?
"How much less could one fail to extract the three types of poisonous arrows when they are explained in detail?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"As I have previously stated, a bhikṣu of pure precepts can act according to his heart's desire by virtue of his original vows."
All Buddhas possess this Dharma, namely, the Great Dharma Drum Sūtra on non-action, non-arising, and non-extinction. Therefore, Kāśyapa,
in a future age you shall also be like me.
Why is this? If any of the fourfold assembly hears your name, the three kinds of poisonous arrows will all be extracted. Therefore, Kāśyapa!
“You should now inquire about the Mahābherīhāraka-sūtra, so that after my parinirvāṇa it may be protected, upheld, and proclaimed throughout the world for a long time.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha,
saying, “Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"Now you should explain the Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra for me.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Regarding the Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra, you should ask few questions."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I shall now set forth my doubts.”
“As the World-Honored One has said: ‘If there is existence, there is suffering and pleasure; if there is no existence, there is neither suffering nor pleasure.
What is the meaning of this? The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“‘No existence’ refers to the supreme bliss of parinirvāṇa. Therefore, by being free from suffering and pleasure, one attains the supreme bliss of parinirvāṇa.”
Whether it be suffering or pleasure, these are existence.
If there were no existence, there would be neither suffering nor pleasure.
Therefore, those who wish to attain parinirvāṇa should seek to sever existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All that exists is impermanent, And there is nothing that does not change.
That which exists has suffering and pleasure; That which does not exist has neither suffering nor pleasure."
There is no suffering or pleasure for one who does not act; when one acts, there is suffering and pleasure.
Do not delight in conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*), nor should you ever again associate with them.
Even if a person attains peace and happiness, they may fall back into suffering once more.
"If one does not reach nirvāṇa, one does not abide in the place of peace and bliss.
At that time, Kāśyapa replied in verse:
"Sentient beings do not exist [as real entities]; nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss."
"That is merely the pleasure of names; there is no one who experiences pleasure.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Perpetual liberation is not a name; the wondrous form abides in profound stillness."
"It is not the realm of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How can you say that form is yet eternally abiding?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall now provide an analogy."
It is as if a man were to come from the south, from Mathurā,
and someone were to ask him:
"From where have you come?"
The man replied, "I have come from Mathurā.
He was then asked again:
“Where is Mathurā located?
At that time, the man pointed toward the south.
“Kāśyapa! [he said.]
Is it not because that person has gained faith in this? Why is that?
It is because that man saw him coming for himself.
"In this way, Kāśyapa,
because of my vision, you should have faith in me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a man might point to the sky with his finger,
so too do I now describe liberation through names.
It is like that man who has come from afar from the south."
Now I am likewise thus, having emerged from that nirvana. Furthermore,
Kāśyapa, for one who perceives the true meaning, there is no need for causes and conditions.
If one does not perceive the meaning, then causes and conditions are required.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly reveal liberation through immeasurable causes and conditions.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha,
saying, "What is the cause?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The cause is this matter.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What constitutes the condition?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The 'condition' (pratyaya) is that which is relied upon.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May you further reveal what this analogy is.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is like a child being born from a mother and a father; the mother is the cause, and the father is the condition.”
"Therefore, parents provide the conditions for the birth of a child.
To speak of phenomena arising through such causes and conditions is what is called 'accomplishment.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the meaning of 'accomplishment'?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"'Accomplishment' refers to the accomplishment of the world."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by 'the world'?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Sentient beings are a conventional designation for a combination of factors.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by ‘sentient beings’?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is the ‘Provisioning of the Collection of Dharmas.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'Dharma'?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That which is non-Dharma is also Dharma, and that which is Dharma is also non-Dharma."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of phenomena (*dharma*). What are these two?
They are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and form (*rūpa*) and the formless (*arūpa*); there is no third phenomenon beyond these.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is the likeness of the Dharma?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The Dharma is not form.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What category does non-Dharma belong to?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That which is non-dharma is also not form.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If dharmas and non-dharmas are neither form nor signless, how can they be dharmas?
How can they be non-dharmas?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Dharma is nirvāṇa; non-Dharma is existence.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If Dharma and non-Dharma are neither form nor characteristics, how does the wise one know them?”
"What is it that is known?
For what reason is that characteristic known?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"When sentient beings undergo birth and death, the cultivation of various merits and pure roots of goodness constitutes their correct practice.
If they practice such dharmas, all marks of purity will arise;
those who practice these dharmas are 'sentient beings of this dharma'."
Sentient beings, within the cycle of birth and death, perform various kinds of non-meritorious, evil, and unwholesome deeds.
If they practice such unrighteousness, all manner of evil and impure signs arise;
those who practice this unrighteousness are unrighteous sentient beings.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘sentient beings’?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Sentient beings are designated as being comprised of the four elements—namely, the internal earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element—as well as the sense bases of the five faculties, up to the thirteen links of dependent origination. As stated in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
'Ignorance arises from improper mental attention.'"
"Therefore, among the thirteen links, feeling, perception, volition, mind, consciousness, and mental awareness—these are called the phenomena of sentient beings.
Kāśyapa, you should know that these are called all phenomena."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Among these, what dharma is a sentient being?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In this regard, there is not even a single dharma that is called a 'sentient being.
Why is this so? Kāśyapa!"
"For example, King Prasenajit has a drum. What constitutes a drum?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha, "That which is called a drum consists of leather, wood, and a mallet; the combination of these three factors is what is named a drum."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In this way, the conventional designation of a combination is called a 'sentient being.

"This multitude is exhausted and may soon turn back.
In order to provide them with a place of rest, he conjured a great city ahead on the road and pointed it out from afar to the great assembly, saying:
"There is a great city ahead; you must go there quickly.
As the entire multitude saw themselves gradually drawing near to that city, they said to one another, "This is our place of rest."
They immediately entered the city together to rest and enjoy themselves; delighting in staying there, they had no desire to proceed further.
At that time, the guide thought to himself:
"This great multitude has obtained this minor pleasure and considers it sufficient; they have become weak and indolent, lacking the intent to advance."
At that time, the guide immediately caused the conjured city to vanish.
When the great assembly saw the city disappear, they addressed the guide, saying: "What was this?"
"Is it an illusion? Is it a dream? Or is it reality?
Having heard this, the Teacher immediately addressed the great assembly:
"The great city you saw earlier was merely a transformation created by me for the sake of providing rest.
There is yet another city where we must now go; you should proceed there quickly for the sake of happiness and peace."
The great assembly replied:
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
For what reason do you delight in this inferior and lowly place?"
"Let us proceed together toward the Great City of Peace and Bliss.
The guide replied, "Excellent; let us go."
They immediately proceeded forward together.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"The preliminary signs of the great city we are headed for have already appeared; you should observe them, for that great city ahead is exceedingly prosperous and joyful."
Advancing gradually, they beheld that great city.
At that time, the guide addressed the great assembly:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that this is the great city."

At that time, the great assembly, seeing from afar that the great city was peaceful, secure, prosperous, and joyful, felt gladness in their hearts; they looked at one another and gave rise to a sense of wonder, thinking:
"Is this city real?"
"Or is it a false illusion?
The Guide replied, "This city is real; it is entirely extraordinary, peaceful, secure, and prosperous."
He then addressed that multitude:
"Enter this great city; this is the foremost, ultimate great city, and beyond this place there is no other city."
Once that great assembly had all entered the city, they were filled with a sense of wonder and their hearts rejoiced;
they praised that guide, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
"True great wisdom and the skillful means of great compassion have taken pity on us.

Kāśyapa, you should know that the initial "city of transformation" refers to the pure wisdom of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—the wisdom of liberation characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the true great city is the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Tathāgata reveals the three vehicles and manifests two types of nirvāṇa, yet he also speaks of the one vehicle.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who say that this sutra does not exist, they are not my disciples, nor am I their teacher."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Many Mahāyāna sūtras extensively expound the meaning of emptiness.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“All sūtras concerning emptiness are teachings with further meaning to be explained; only this sūtra is the unsurpassed teaching, not one that leaves further meaning to be explained.”

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, it is like King Prasenajit, who regularly holds a great assembly for almsgiving in the eleventh month; first he feeds the hungry ghosts, the solitary, and the poor beggars, and subsequently bestows sweet delicacies of various flavors upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas according to their desires.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise in this regard: in accordance with the various inclinations and desires of sentient beings, they expound various sūtras and teachings.

If there are sentient beings who are indolent and violate the precepts, who do not diligently practice, and who abandon the eternally abiding, wondrous scripture of the Tathāgatagarbha to take pleasure in studying various sūtras on emptiness—either explaining them according to the literal words and phrases, or adding and altering those words and phrases.
Why is this? For they speak thus:
"All Buddhist sūtras teach that there is no self."
Yet they do not understand the meaning of emptiness and non-self; those people lacking wisdom proceed toward cessation.
Nevertheless, this teaching of emptiness and non-self is also the word of the Buddha. Why is that?
The immeasurable dust and defilements, the storehouse of all afflictions, are eternally empty in *nirvāṇa*; such *nirvāṇa* is the phrase for "all things.
That which is eternally abiding in peace and bliss is the phrase for the Great Parinirvāṇa attained by the Buddha.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does one depart from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"As long as sentient beings cycle through birth and death, they lack self-mastery; for this reason, I have taught the meaning of non-self."
"However, the Great Parinirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas is eternally abiding and blissful; for this reason, it destroys those notions of annihilation and permanence.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have long since turned away from the notion of no-self and turned toward the self.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is in order to destroy the 'self' of worldly beings that I teach the meaning of no-self."
If one were not to speak in this manner, how could one cause them to receive the Dharma of the Great Teacher?

When the Buddha teaches non-self, those sentient beings conceive a sense of wonder at something they have never heard before; they come to where the Buddha is and, thereafter, through hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions, are led to enter the Buddha-Dharma.

Once they have entered the Buddha-dharma, their faith increases; they diligently cultivate vigor and skillfully study the dharma of emptiness. Only then do you preach for them the liberation that is eternally abiding, blissful, and possessed of form.
Furthermore, there are some worldly people who claim that there is such a thing as liberation; in order to refute them, it is said that liberation is entirely non-existent.
If one were not to speak in this way, how could one cause them to accept the Dharma of the Great Teacher?
Therefore, through hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions, I teach liberation as the cessation and extinction of the non-self.

Subsequently, I see those beings who regard ultimate extinction as liberation; those people lacking wisdom pursue such extinction. Thereafter, I again teach through hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions that liberation does indeed exist.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who have attained liberation and mastery should know that sentient beings must necessarily possess permanence.”
For example, just as one who sees smoke necessarily knows there is fire, if there were a self, there would necessarily be liberation.

To say that there is a self is already to say that liberation possesses form; it is neither the mundane view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), nor is it a teaching of annihilationism or eternalism.
Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How is it that the Tathāgata, though not entering parinirvāṇa, manifests parinirvāṇa; and though unborn, manifests birth?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In order to destroy the sentient beings' conception of permanence, the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa yet manifests entering parinirvāṇa; he is unborn yet manifests birth."
Why is this so? Because sentient beings think that even the Buddha is subject to death and lacks mastery; how much more so for us, who possess the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self"?
It is like a king who has been captured by a neighboring country, bound and shackled, and reflects thus:
"Am I now still a king, am I still a lord?
I am now neither king nor lord.
For what reason have such calamities as these come upon me?"
"Because of negligence.
In this way, sentient beings wander through the cycle of birth and death until they lack self-mastery;
because they lack self-mastery, the meaning of "non-self" is taught.
For example, suppose there were a person being pursued by a thief who, raising a sword, intended to kill him; this person would think:

"I now lack the power to escape this mortal peril. Just as one might conceive such thoughts, so too do sentient beings, conditioned by the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, give rise to the thought: "May I become Śakra or Brahmā."
In order to destroy that misconception, the Tathāgata manifests death.
The Tathāgata is the God among gods; if he were to enter parinirvāṇa and be utterly extinguished, the world would perish.
If he does not perish, then he dwells eternally in peace and bliss.
If there were permanent and blissful existence, there would necessarily be a self, just as smoke implies fire.
Furthermore, if one were to claim there is a self where there is no self, the world would be filled with such selves; yet this is not the case.
Nor is it that the absence of a self is destroyed. If there truly were no self, then the concept of a "self" could not be established.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is that which ‘exists’?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"That which 'exists' refers to the conduct of sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of existence;
that which 'does not exist' refers to insentient things."
If these sentient beings did not exist, they would have to come from elsewhere.
Furthermore, if there were things that could be destroyed through volition, sentient beings would decrease;
yet if these sentient beings did not exist, they would instead be fully pervasive.
"Because sentient beings are neither born nor destroyed, they neither decrease nor increase.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“If there were a self, how could those afflictions and various defilements arise?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent, excellent!”
You should ask the Tathāgata this very question.
It is like a goldsmith who, seeing the nature of gold, reflects thus:
"By what cause does this nature of gold become defiled?"
"Now we must investigate the root from which this defilement arises.
"How would that person succeed in finding its root? Kāśyapa replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"If one contemplates the primary causal signs throughout the duration of one's life, will one ever reach the original limit from which there is no beginning?
Since the original limit cannot be found, neither can gold be found."
"If one employs skillful means and applies oneself with diligent effort without slackening, one can remove those impurities from the gold; only then will one obtain the gold.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In this same way, I am born with adventitious afflictions."
One who wishes to see me should reflect thus:
"Now I must investigate the root of both the self and defilement.
Would such a person succeed in finding that root?
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If one diligently applies skillful means to remove the defilements of affliction, only then will one attain me.
This means hearing a sūtra such as this, believing and delighting in it with a profound mind, being neither lax nor hasty, employing skillful means, and single-mindedly perfecting the three karmas."
"By these causes and conditions, I have finally attained my attainment.
Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there were a self, why is it not seen?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall now provide an analogy."
For example, when a beginner learns the five-character verse that forms a complete stanza,
they wish to know its meaning beforehand before they begin their study.
Would they be able to know it?
One must first train, and only then will one come to know.

Once they have trained well, the teacher then instructs them on the formation of phrases and meanings within the realms, illustrating them through analogies, and they are able to listen and receive [the teaching].
Because they obtain the understanding of the boundaries of the Dharma through their teachers, they are able to have faith and joy.
Thus, for the sake of sentient beings shrouded by the storehouse of afflictions, I now say: "Good sons!..."
"The Tathāgatagarbha is thus and so.
He then wishes to see it;
will he be able to see it?
Kāśyapa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Just as those who do not understand the meaning of the phrases regarding the formation of realms should rely on faith in their teacher, so too, Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is one who speaks words of truth; it is with words of truth that he says there are sentient beings."
"You shall know this later when you have completed your training.

Now, for your sake, I shall further provide an analogy, like the four analogies for the concealment of the realm of sentient beings: namely, the film covering the eye, the thick clouds obscuring the moon, a person digging a well, and the lamp-flame within a jar. You should know that these four possess the causal conditions for the Buddha-treasure."
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, adorned and illuminated by immeasurable marks and signs; because of that nature, all sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa."
Just as that cataract of the eye is a curable disease, yet the eyes remain perpetually dark until one encounters a skilled physician;
once a skilled physician is encountered, one quickly regains the sight of forms.

In the same way, the storehouse of immeasurable afflictions obscures the *tathāgatagarbha*, such that until one encounters the Buddhas, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*, one reckons "self," "non-self," and "what belongs to the self" as being the self.
If one encounters the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas, one then realizes the true self; it is like the recovery from an illness, whereby one's vision becomes clear and bright.
"Cataracts" refers to the various afflictions (*kleśa*), while "the eye" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*.
"Just as the moon is not bright and pure when covered by clouds,
so too the Tathāgata-nature is not bright and pure when shrouded by the storehouse of afflictions.
If one is freed from the cloud-like covering of all afflictions, the nature of the Tathāgata is as pure as the full moon."
"It is like a person digging a well: if they encounter dry earth, they know the water is still far off;
if they encounter moist earth and mud, they know the water is gradually near;
if they reach the water itself, that is the ultimate goal."
In this way, by encountering the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, one cultivates wholesome conduct, excavates the soil of afflictions, and attains the water of the Tathāgata-nature.
It is like the flame of a lamp inside a jar: its light does not manifest and is of no use to sentient beings;
yet if the jar is broken, its radiance shines everywhere.

In this way, when the lamp of the Tathāgatagarbha is covered by the jar of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), its marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) are not bright or pure and are of no use to sentient beings;

yet, if it is freed from the storehouse of all afflictions, that Tathāgata-nature’s afflictions are forever exhausted, and its marks and signs shine forth to perform the Buddha-work, just as the lamp from a broken jar is enjoyed by sentient beings.

"By means of these four kinds of analogies and causes and conditions, just as I have a realm of sentient beings, you should know that all sentient beings are likewise so; that realm of sentient beings is boundless, luminous, and pure."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha as a single nature and a single vehicle, for what reason does the Tathāgata speak of three vehicles—the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall now provide an analogy.
Suppose there is a very wealthy elder who has an only son; while following his nurse, the child becomes lost amidst a great crowd."
As the elder was approaching his death, he reflected:
"I have long since lost my only son; I have no other sons, nor parents, nor relatives. Once I pass away, the king will take all my wealth and property."
While he was thus reflecting, his son, whom he had lost, while wandering about begging for alms, arrived at his own home; yet he did not recognize it as his father’s house. Why was this so?
Because he was lost at a young age,
his father recognized him but did not claim him as his son. Why was this?
Because he was fleeing out of fear and anxiety, [the man] gave him much wealth and said to him:
"I have no offspring; act as my son and do not go elsewhere."
The son replied: "I am unable to dwell here. Why is that? Because—"
"Living here in constant suffering, as if bound in fetters.
The elder said to him, "What do you wish to do?"
The son replied again:
"I would rather remove various impurities, tend cattle, and work in the fields.
The elder thought to himself:
"This son has little merit; I shall know the proper time. For now, let him follow his own inclination.
He then ordered him to remove refuse.
After a long time, the son saw the great elder enjoying himself with the five desires, and a sense of joy arose in his heart. He then reflected thus:
"May the Great Elder deign to take pity on me and accept me, granting me much wealth and treasure so that I may become your son.
Having formed this thought, he no longer applied himself to his labors.
Having seen him, the elder thought to himself:
"Before long, he will surely become my son.
At that time, the elder immediately addressed him, saying:
"Why do you now give rise to such contrary thoughts and fail to apply yourself diligently to your work?
He replied, "I wish to become your son; it is with this intention that I have formed this thought."
The elder said, "Excellent. I am your father, and you are my son."
"I am truly your father, yet you did not know it; I now entrust all my treasuries and storehouses to you.
Then, in the midst of the great assembly, he proclaimed these words:
"This is my son. I lost him long ago, and though he has now encountered me and returned home, he was unaware of it himself."
"I have treated you as my son, yet you were unwilling; today you have come of your own accord to seek to be my son.
"Kāśyapa! Just as that elder used skillful means to entice his son of inferior disposition, first making him remove dung and only later entrusting him with the wealth."
In the midst of the great assembly, he spoke these words:
"This was originally my son; lost for a long time, he has fortunately come of his own accord today to be my son."
"Kāśyapa! For those who do not delight in the One Vehicle (ekayāna), I teach the Three Vehicles (triyāna). Why is this? Because..."
"This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means.
All these śrāvakas are my sons; they are like those who remove filth, who have only now come to know it for themselves.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Alas, how strange! This Śrāvaka vehicle—how exceedingly base it is!
Truly they are sons of the Buddha, yet they do not recognize their father."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should train yourself in this way.
If you cannot endure being rebuked or reviled, then you should abandon [such persons]."
"When they ripen in the future, you shall know them. Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
the Śrāvaka and the Mahāyāna are constantly at variance— worldly versus outflow-free, delusion versus wisdom.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, those who slander this sutra should be gathered in. Why is that? Because..."
Because of that slander, upon casting off this body, they shall fall into boundless darkness.
Out of compassion for them, you should employ skillful means to bring them to maturity through the Mahāyāna Dharma.
If they are incurable, they shall fall into hell;
if there are those with faith, they shall believe of their own accord;
as for the remaining sentient beings, one should gather them through the means of attraction and lead them to liberation.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if there is a man who has first contracted a fever, one should not administer medicine or any other treatment to him. Why is that? Because—"
Because the time has not yet arrived;
one must wait for the time to come before treating it. If one does not know these two points, they are a failed physician.
Therefore, one should treat the illness only after it has matured.
If that which is not yet mature must wait for the time to arrive,
so it is with sentient beings who slander this sutra: when their transgressions reach maturity, they will deeply repent and reproach themselves,
saying, "Alas, what suffering!"
"What I have done, I have only now begun to realize.
At that time, one should rescue and sustain them by means of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). "Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
Suppose there were a man crossing a vast wilderness who heard the cries of a flock of birds.

At that time, the man, reflecting on those bird sounds, thought there were bandits and took a different path; he entered an empty marsh and reached a place where tigers and wolves dwell, only to be devoured by a tiger.

In this way, Kāśyapa, those future bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās will, regarding the sounds of "self" and "non-self," fear the sound of "self" and fall into the nihilistic view of great emptiness by practicing non-self; they will fail to give rise to faith or delight in such profound sūtras concerning the Tathāgatagarbha and the eternal abiding of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, regarding what you asked me concerning my teaching for Ānanda:
'Where there is existence, there is suffering and pleasure; where there is no existence, there is neither suffering nor pleasure.'"
"Listen attentively now, Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata is neither existent nor a sentient being, nor is he subject to destruction."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: “How is this so,
World-Honored One?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suppose beneath the Snowy Mountains there is the nature of a maṇi-jewel that emits pure light.
If there is a person who well understands the characteristics of maṇi-jewels, they will recognize it upon seeing its signs, immediately take it up, and carry it away."
It is like the method of refining gold: once the dross has been eliminated, it becomes free from defilement and pure; wherever it is applied, its original impurities do not stain it. Why is this?
It is like a man carrying a lamp while walking: wherever he goes, all darkness is dispelled, and the light of the lamp shines with particular brilliance.

That mani-jewel is likewise: like refined gold that cannot be defiled by dust or grime, when illuminated by the light of the stars and moon it rains down pure water, and when struck by the rays of the sun it immediately emits fire.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he is forever free from all birth, old age, sickness, and death; the afflictions and the stains of habitual tendencies are entirely extinguished. He is always a great illumination, like that bright jewel which cannot be defiled by anything;
he is like a pure lotus flower, upon which dust and water do not cling.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, at such and such times and in such and such forms, the Tathāgata appears in the world; according to what is appropriate for them, he manifests an ordinary body, yet he is not defiled by the impurities of those various ordinary birthplaces, nor does he experience the worldly suffering or pleasure."
"Bliss consists of the fivefold qualities of sensual desire for humans and devas; these are themselves suffering. Only liberation is ultimate and eternal bliss.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
"World-Honored One!
Reflecting upon myself, it was only now that I first left the household life, received full ordination, attained the status of a bhikṣu, and became an arhat.
I ought to acknowledge and repay the kindness of the Tathāgata—for it was the Tathāgata who, in days past, shared half of his seat with me."
"Today, once again, amidst the four great assemblies, the water of the Mahāyāna Dharma has been poured upon my crown.

At that time, within the assembly, there were some who assumed the appearance and deportment of bhikṣus, some who assumed the appearance and deportment of upāsakas, and some who assumed the appearance and deportment of those who were not upāsakas; they leaned, tilted, lowered, and raised themselves—all of which was the work of Māra.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This great assembly has now been cleared of all chaff and husks; it is firm, solid, and true, like a grove of sandalwood trees."
"In such an assembly, how does he abide?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Ask Mahākāśyapa."
Ānanda said, “Yes. Excellent! I shall ask.”
He then asked Kāśyapa, "In this assembly, how does he abide? Kāśyapa replied:
"That foolish person is a follower of Māra; he has come together with Māra.
Therefore, Ānanda, I have previously said: "
"Unable to bear the responsibility of skillfully protecting and upholding the True Dharma after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, as one would carefully guard a field.
For this reason, it was previously said:
"It would be better to carry the great earth," as explained at length above.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to me, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you shall endure and protect the True Dharma until its final extinction.
I then addressed the Buddha:
"I am capable of protecting and upholding the True Dharma for forty years.
At that time, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"Why are you so indolent as to be unable to protect the Dharma until its very end?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should first seek out Māra.
If you are able to find him, you will be capable of protecting the Dharma."
Kāśyapa then observed with his divine eye, yet he was unable to see him.
It was like a rustic man from Śrāvastī who had lost his son; searching for his son among the great assembly, he could not find him and returned home exhausted.
Kāśyapa’s inability to find Māra within the great assembly with his divine eye was likewise.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I am not capable of searching for the evil Māra.”
Thus, these eighty great śrāvakas all said, "We are not capable.
He then commanded five hundred bodhisattvas, led by Bhadrapāla— with the exception of one bodhisattva named Sarvalokapriyadarśana— to search for the evil Māra, yet they too could not find him.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa:
"You are not capable of protecting and upholding the True Dharma during the final eighty years when the Dharma is about to perish.
A Bodhisattva from the south shall be able to protect and uphold it; you should seek him out among the five hundred followers of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla as the very last."
Kāśyapa replied: "Excellent!
We shall seek him; we have found the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana, World-Honored One."
"The Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana is that very person.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Go and entreat him, and have him seek out the Evil Māra."
At that time, Kāśyapa, together with eighty great śrāvakas and five hundred bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla, all joined in exhorting the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana: "O youth!..."
“The one whom the World-Honored One has designated is capable of seeking out Māra.
At that time, the youth addressed Kāśyapa in the midst of the great assembly, saying,
“I am now able to go forth and seek out Māra.”

Yet there are eighty great śrāvakas, five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Bhadrapāla, as well as Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others; for what reason do they not seek [him], but instead cause me to seek him?
"It would be fitting to let him go first,
and only then reach me. Kāśyapa said to him,
"Is it not a blessing to have subdued Māra?"
He replied: "Kāśyapa!
You know what constitutes merit; you should practice it yourself."
"I am currently unable to do so.
At that time, Kāśyapa reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“What was said by this youth?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“The youth spoke thus:”
"First were the various great virtuous ones, and only then did it reach me.
I am a layperson, and my nature is furthermore lowly and inferior.
These various great virtuous ones, the eighty śrāvakas, and the five hundred leaders such as Bhadrapāla—all of them were first, and only after them did it come to me."
At that time, all the śrāvakas and Bhadrapāla and the others searched everywhere, yet none could find him— just as those wild folk who sought their child but did not obtain it—
and they all said, "We are unable."
Standing to one side, the World-Honored One then addressed Kāśyapa again:

"Now that you have heard this Mahādharmadundubhi Sūtra, during the forty years following my parinirvāṇa, you shall skillfully protect and uphold the True Dharma as it is now; you shall beat the great Dharma drum, blow the great Dharma conch, convene the great Dharma assembly, and erect the great Dharma banner."

Thereafter, when eighty years remain before the True Dharma is extinguished, the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana shall bind that evil Māra and his retinue with fivefold bonds as if binding a small rabbit; he shall extensively proclaim the Mahādharmabherī-sūtra, beat the great Dharma drum, blow the great Dharma conch, establish the great Dharma assembly, and raise the great Dharma banner.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"At what time shall this occur?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The True Dharma will remain for eighty years before its extinction.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to see the Evil Māra.
The Buddha told the youth,
"Quickly show the Evil Māra to the great assembly."
At that time, the youth gazed up at the World-Honored One and pointed him out, saying:
"Behold this evil Māra, who has come from another direction; like the various bodhisattvas, he has assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu and sits among the assembly."
The great assembly all saw him bound by the five fetters. Māra said: "O youth!
"I shall no longer create obstacles for this sutra.
Thus he spoke three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, including the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana, saying:
“Mahākāśyapa has already been able to protect and uphold the True Dharma for forty years after my parinirvāṇa; among you, who is able to be the last to protect the Dharma after my passing?”
When he had spoken thus three times, there was no one capable of accepting it.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Do not give rise to thoughts of inferiority or inadequacy."
Within this assembly of mine, there are many disciples who, after my parinirvāṇa, will be able to protect the true Dharma and preach this sutra.

Among them, the last of the five hundred bodhisattvas, including Bhadrapāla and others—the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana—shall, after my parinirvāṇa, beat the great Dharma drum, blow the great Dharma conch, convene the great Dharma assembly, and raise the great Dharma banner.
At that time, the youth immediately released Māra the Evil One.
Then the great assembly said to the youth:
"You have already received your prediction."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Now, Kāśyapa!
You are like a farmer who lacks skillful means; you are not capable of protecting and upholding this sutra."

Now that this youth, having heard this sutra, is able to recite it well, maintains it before him, and expounds it for others, constantly manifests in the body of an ordinary person while dwelling in the seventh stage.

When eighty years remained before the True Dharma was to perish, he was born in the village of Mahāpāli in the kingdom of Maṇḍala in the south, on the banks of the river Suparikarma, into the Kātyāyana clan.

"You should become a bhikṣu bearing my name and, like one employing skillful means to protect the sprouts in a field, leave the secular world to renounce the householder's life among those who are lax with pride and indolent, and gather that assembly through the four methods of attraction."
Having obtained this profound sutra, they shall recite and master it thoroughly, causing the Sangha to become pure and leading them to relinquish the previously received fundamentally impure objects.

For their sake, they shall preach the *Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra*; secondly, they shall preach the Mahayana Sutra on Emptiness; and thirdly, they shall preach the *Sattvadhātu-tathāgatātyantasthiti-mahābherī-haraka-sūtra*, beating the great Dharma drum, blowing the great Dharma conch, convening the great Dharma assembly, and erecting the great Dharma banner.
Before me, you shall don the armor of the great vow and, throughout the full span of a hundred years, constantly rain down the rain of Dharma and expound this sutra.
When the hundred years have passed, manifesting great supernormal powers, you shall demonstrate parinirvāṇa and deliver this prediction:
"The Buddha Śākyamuni has now come here; all should gaze upon him with reverence and pay him homage."
"In this way, the Tathāgata eternally dwells in peace and bliss; you, sirs, should contemplate true permanence and bliss as I have explained.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared in person within the sky and spoke these words: "So it is, so it is!"
"As you have said, all should believe in these well-spoken words.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By accomplishing how many virtues can a bodhisattva perceive the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding and indestructible Dharma-body, and manifest great supernormal powers at the time of death?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who accomplishes eight virtues can directly perceive the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding and indestructible Dharma-body.”
What are these eight?
First, when expounding this profound sutra, the mind remains free from indolence.
Second, when expounding the three types of teachings of the Three Vehicles, one likewise remains free from weariness.
Third, they never abandon those who are to be transformed.
Fourth, if the Saṃgha is divided, they bring about reconciliation and unify it in a single flavor.
Fifth, they never associate with bhikṣuṇīs, women, or eunuchs.
Sixth, to stay far away from associating with kings and those of great power.
Seventh, to always delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Eighth, to contemplate and investigate impurity and non-self (*anātman*).
These are the eight kinds of meritorious qualities that are accomplished.
Furthermore, there are four matters. What are these four?
First, they are well able to uphold the Dharma.
Second, they constantly rejoice within themselves, saying: "Excellent!
"What I have now done is a great and wholesome happiness.
Third, one is able to take refuge for oneself, thinking:
"I have attained a beneficial gain."
"Fourth, one is free from doubt regarding the eternal abiding of the Tathāgata and constantly recollects the Tathāgata’s merits day and night.
By these causes and conditions, one will manifest before the eyes the eternally abiding Dharmakāya displaying great supernormal powers, and only then pass away."
“Kāśyapa! In this way, wherever these sons and daughters of good family dwell—in cities, towns, or villages—I manifest the Dharma-body for their sake and speak these words:
‘Sons of good family!’”
"O virtuous woman!
The Tathāgata abides eternally.
From this day forward, you should constantly receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and explain it to others, speaking these words:"
"You should know that the Tathāgata eternally abides in peace and bliss; with a right mind and sincere aspiration, do not be deceitful or crooked.
You should know that the World-Honored One thus eternally abides; to those who possess pure aspiration, I shall manifest my body."
"Mahākāśyapa, you should believe and examine this: if one does not practice the Dharma in such a manner, by what means could one see me?
How could one possibly attain the manifestation of supernatural powers?"
Just as I have declared for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle that if a bhikṣu is able to relinquish a single dharma, I guarantee that he will attain the fruit of Anāgāmin—
so too is it with the accomplishment of the merits of his practice.

As I have previously stated, the devas constantly follow and serve a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts throughout his life; therefore, you should not crave gain and offerings, but should instead cultivate disenchantment and dwell in the application of mindfulness to the body.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a bhikṣu who upholds my name shall always cause the Saṃgha to be pure.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What does this mean?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"When they practice grasping, they will satisfy the flocks of greedy crows who violate the precepts, just as those [previous ones] skillfully guarded the four dharmas.
Those such as Bhadrapāla and the five hundred bodhisattvas were previously unable to do so; even now, they are still unable to protect the Dharma at the end after my parinirvāṇa."

When the bhikṣu who upholds my name practices the dharma of gathering [the community], he shall gather those bhikṣus who are lax and indolent; he shall provide them with offerings, give them sūtra scrolls, and sustain them through careful guidance and protection.
Just as in the method of raising oxen, one knows when they are ready to be subdued and only then tames them.
If one takes them in for training and they do not reform, then one simply abandons them, so that their poisonous arrows do not wound the pure and wholesome [mind].
He should further reflect in this way:
"Let it not be that a bhikṣu of pure conduct is affected by his transgression of the precepts.

One who speaks what is not the Dharma and practices evil conduct should not be paid homage; one should not participate with him in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha, such as the Dharma-meeting, the Poṣadha, the Pravarana, or the Karmavācanā; in all matters, one should not associate with him."
"Just as the king subdued his enemies, so too did he.

Having thus tamed them through skillful means, for a hundred years he constantly rained down the rain of Dharma, beat the great drum of Dharma, blew the great conch of Dharma, established the great assembly of Dharma, raised the great banner of Dharma, and displayed great supernormal powers, until his life ended in parinirvāṇa."

After more than a thousand Buddhas and sixty-two kalpas had passed, and following the parinirvāṇa of hundreds of thousands of pratyekabuddhas and eight Tathāgatas, he then attained the Way of the Buddha, named Jñānaskandhaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The bhikṣu who at that time bore my name was none other than the Licchavi youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana; he shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment in this very land.
“Kāśyapa, you should know that unsurpassed bodhi is thus difficult to attain.
Kāśyapa! Is this something that can be attained by an ordinary person?”
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"In one buddha-field, one buddha performs buddha-work; the second and third do likewise.
It is as if within a single mustard seed there are numerous worlds, revolving and circling about without being aware of it."
Who brought it here and went away?
Who placed it here for me?
One should act in accordance with what needs to be known, acting in conformity with that.
Thus, there are some who know me and some who do not.
In this world, upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there is Śākyamuni Buddha; within this very place, there is also the Buddha Ajita.
In this world, he sometimes manifests the conflagration at the end of an eon, and sometimes manifests the preaching of the Dharma; such wonders are truly rare and extraordinary.
Furthermore, what is most supreme and extraordinary?
It is that the youth Sarvalokapriyadarśana was not born into an ordinary household; the family into which he was born consisted entirely of bodhisattvas.
Kāśyapa, you should know that those who provide offerings and attend to him will all be filled with joy; his kinsmen and relatives will cherish him and say:
"Such a person as this has been born within our own lineage."
"All these people have been sent by me.

Kāśyapa, you should know that if those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the other four assemblies, take them as their followers and all hear this Great Dharma Drum Sūtra being preached, they shall all attain unexcelled bodhi."
“Kāśyapa! In the distant past, during a long-ago age, I was a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) in the city of Vaiśālī, named Nandiṣeṇa.
At that time, the city of Vaiśālī was like Jambudvīpa when the Four Heavenly Kings descend to it, or like the Sahā world; the other worlds were likewise so, as was this entire trichiliocosm.”
At that time, my lifespan was inconceivable.

As such a Wheel-Turning Sage King, I practiced incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and supreme acts of giving and various meritorious deeds; I maintained pure ethical discipline and cultivated all manner of wholesome conduct, thereby amassing such immeasurable merit and virtue.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great Dharma Drum being preached, even if they go there with a playful or mocking mind for as little as a single thought-moment, the merit they obtain will surpass the previous meritorious deeds; it is beyond measure or record, and cannot be calculated by means of numbers, analogies, or metaphors.
Suppose there were a king of mantras named Jvalanaprabha; by reciting this mantra once, one would be well protected for four months.

Kāśyapa, you should know that such is the power of ordinary worldly mantras; how much more so, then, could the power of reading the Great Dharma Drum Sūtra not provide protection for the remainder of one's life?

Therefore, those sentient beings who are able to make offerings to this sutra establish a decisive cause for unexcelled bodhi; until they reach ultimate bodhi, they shall never be separated from this sutra.
Then the great assembly raised their voices in unison, crying out:
"Excellent, excellent! How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
Now this youth shall become a bhikṣu who upholds the names of the Buddhas; if he were to enter parinirvāṇa, the deities of the Jeta Grove would have no one to rely upon. Why is this so?
"He came from the south to the place where the Buddha was and entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told the great assembly:
"He did not come; rather, I went to him myself, manifesting my body there. I first dispatched this sutra, and only then did I go."
Why is this? If this sutra does not reach their hands, they will give rise to a mind of retreat.
If there are sentient beings therein who should be tamed, I, together with the great assembly, shall go and stand before them.
Upon seeing me, he shall immediately return to welcome me and then enter parinirvāṇa, entering parinirvāṇa wherever he wishes to deliver sentient beings.
At that time, the son of Śakra, named Abhimanyu, shall come here by means of his supernormal powers.
Although he is young, his true mind is pure and he has faith and delight in the Mahāyāna;
he stands alone without equal among gods and humans, upholding this profound Mahāyāna sūtra. For this reason, he is taught the cause of liberation and receives the prophecy of Buddhahood.
Then the great assembly spoke these verses with one voice:
"How marvelous! All beings, who are a joy for the world to behold!"
Appearing in the form of a bhikṣu, he beats the great Dharma drum, protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure for a long time.
After his parinirvāṇa, the world will become empty;
after his passing into extinction, there shall be none equal to him.
"Such a bhikṣu is rare to find in the world; he is able to proclaim for the sake of the world the path to the ultimate goal.
At that time, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, and the great assembly of immeasurable beings, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
